headline: Westpac's credit impairment charge fell $113 million to $424 million in FY25 from $537 million in FY24, a 21% reduction. The loss rate declined 2 basis points to 5 bps of average loans (from 7 bps). The improvement was driven primarily by a $174 million favourable shift in individually assessed provisions — write-backs rose $102 million to $195 million and recoveries rose $57 million to $247 million, partly offset by new IAPs falling only $15 million to $408 million. This was partially offset by a $61 million adverse move in collectively assessed provisions, where write-offs rose $75 million to $561 million, partly offset by other CAP changes improving $14 million to a $103 million benefit. Divisionally, Consumer improved $31 million ($217m vs $248m), Institutional improved $121 million ($1m benefit vs $120m charge), and New Zealand improved $66 million ($41m benefit vs $25m charge), while Business & Wealth worsened $103 million ($245m vs $142m) due to higher overlays, downside scenario increases, and new IAPs in wholesale & retail trade.

drivers.narrative: Write-backs rose $102 million to $195 million and recoveries rose $57 million to $247 million, delivering a combined $159 million improvement. Write-backs were mostly in the wholesale & retail trade and manufacturing sectors; recoveries were mostly within the credit cards and personal loan portfolios (ev-24).
New IAPs fell $15 million to $408 million (from $423 million), a modest improvement. New IAPs were mostly in the services and wholesale & retail trade sectors and the mortgages portfolio (ev-24).

The net IAP line (new IAPs less write-backs and recoveries) moved from a $140 million charge in FY24 to a $34 million benefit in FY25, a $174 million improvement. This is the sum of the three sub-components above.

Other changes in CAPs improved $14 million to a $103 million benefit (from $89 million). Drivers included: an improved economic outlook for commercial property prices and interest rates; lower mortgage 90+ day delinquencies from 1.05% to 0.70%; a 5 percentage point increase in the downside scenario weight reflecting geopolitical instability; and new portfolio overlays (ev-23).
Write-offs rose $75 million to $561 million (from $486 million), adding to the charge. Write-offs were largely within the credit card and personal loan portfolios (ev-22).

The bank states that new portfolio overlays contributed to the higher CAP charge but does not disclose a separate quantified figure for overlays within the 'other changes in CAPs' line. Overlays on the balance sheet rose $59 million to $238 million (ev-21 context).
Total CAPs worsened $61 million to a $458 million charge (from $397 million), comprising the $75 million higher write-offs partly offset by the $14 million improvement in other changes in CAPs.

limitations: The investor discussion pack walk chart (p49) covers a half-on-half comparison (2H24 to 2H25), not the FY24-FY25 task comparison, so its bars cannot be used as quantified drivers.

Business & Wealth segment narrative does not separately quantify the overlay, downside scenario, and IAP contributions within its $245 million charge beyond stating they drove the 9 bps widening to 23 bps.
Institutional, New Zealand, and Group Businesses segments lack detailed FY25 vs FY24 impairment narratives explaining the drivers behind their divisional movements.
The provision-type bridge sums exactly to the total movement ($174m IAP improvement minus $61m CAP worsening = $113m total improvement), so no residual is needed.
Basis normalised from 'cash' to 'ex_notables': no page in evidence prints 'cash' beside the movement, and the registry names ex_notables as the bank's headline basis.

evidence_records.quote: Credit impairment charges of $424 million represented 5 basis points of average gross loans compared to 7 basis points of average gross loans in the prior year.
Impairment charges/(benefits) to average loans 5 bps 7 bps (2 bps)

The credit impairment charge of $424 million represented 5 basis points of average loans, down from 7 basis points in the prior year. The lower impairment charge was mainly due to an increase in write-backs and recoveries partly offset by a higher CAP charge.
The CAP charge of $458 million comprised write-offs of $561 million which was partly offset by a benefit in other changes in CAP of $103 million.
Write-offs were largely within the credit card and personal loan portfolios.

The other changes in CAP were due to: • A reduction from an improved economic outlook for commercial property prices and interest rates; • A reduction in mortgage 90+ day delinquencies from 1.05% to 0.70%; • An increase in the downside scenario weight of 5 percentage points reflecting a rise in geopolitical instability; and • An increase for new portfolio overlays.

The IAP benefit of $34 million comprised: • New IAPs of $408 million, mostly in the services and wholesale & retail trade sectors and the mortgages portfolio; • Recoveries of $247 million, mostly within the credit cards and personal loan portfolios; and • Write-backs of $195 million, mostly in the wholesale & retail trade and manufacturing sectors.

Impairment charge of $217 million • Impairment charges to average loans were 4 basis points, down 1 basis point from the prior year. The charge reflects write-offs in cards and personal lending and an increase in the downside scenario weight. This was partly offset by a release of portfolio overlay provisions.

Impairment charge of $245 million • The impairment charge of 23 basis points of average loans compared to 14 basis points in the prior year. The charge reflects higher overlays, an increase in the downside scenario and new IAPs in the wholesale & retail trade sector.
